shots.caption: A datacenter is a building full of computers. They run the apps, websites and AI we use every day.
Electricity comes in from the grid. This campus near Frankfurt used more than any other site in Germany’s register in 2025.

overlay.source: German datacenter register, 2025 · homes: average German household, 3,383 kWh (Destatis, 2021) · phone charge ≈ 16.1 Wh, calculated from Öko-Test

shots.caption: Inside, rows of servers do the computing.

overlay.source: Calculated from FRA21’s reported PUE of 1.25 and its average load vs. 40 MW built (register, 2025)

shots.caption: Almost all of that electricity ends up as heat, and the heat has to leave the building.

overlay.source: Reported by the operator to the German datacenter register, 2025

shots.caption: Coolers on the roof carry the heat away. Here the water stays sealed in the pipes.

overlay.source: FRA21: from its reported water figure (register, 2025) · The Dalles: Google, 2025 · per person: German household average, 126 L a day (UBA)

shots.caption: Other sites evaporate water to cool, like Google’s campus in Oregon. The blue block is one day of it, to scale.

overlay.source: FRA21: from its reported water figure (register, 2025) · The Dalles: Google, 2025 · per person: German household average, 126 L a day (UBA)

shots.caption: How big is that, compared with a whole country?

overlay.source: Germany’s electricity: 526 TWh (UBA, 2025) · all datacenters: 21.3 TWh, an industry estimate (Bitkom/Borderstep)

shots.caption: Now imagine a datacenter built from the best ideas that already exist somewhere, and some that are only promised. It is fictional, placed in northern Sweden.
Its heat is piped into the town’s heating network. But it makes far more heat than a whole town can use.

overlay.source: Fictional campus at full load · Luleå’s district heat: 823 GWh (LuleKraft, 2019)

shots.caption: In blue glass: technology that is only promised, like small nuclear reactors. None powers a datacenter yet.
